source.title: Shaping capabilities with token-level data filtering

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether adversarial fine-tuning can restore medical performance after RMU unlearning, using medical-text loss and a different pretraining-filtering intervention as a robustness comparison.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own RMU adversarial-fine-tuning results. Cited claims about other unlearning attacks are not rows. The main attack results concern fine-tuning on medical text, not activation ablation, quantization, or prompting.
record.test_reason: The study applies RMU to its own from-scratch models (61M to 1.8B, PubMed forget set) and measures how much adversarial fine-tuning on PubMed text restores baseline medical loss. This is a relearning test of RMU (A, B). The pretraining-filtered models are an alternative capability-removal method tested under the same attack (F). The measure is text loss, not targeted-knowledge accuracy.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that document and token filtering are both substantially more robust to adversarial fine-tuning than RMU, and that the gap grows with scale (up to 10× at 1.8B). RMU's loss collapses within a few steps, while filtered models recover gradually. They also note that current unlearning fails against a few fine-tuning steps.
record.recipe_differences: RMU is the post-training unlearning comparator; the study's main intervention is filtering medical tokens or documents during pretraining. The attack fine-tunes on PubMed medical text.
record.method_sensitivity: The relative robustness changes with model scale; the paper reports a widening advantage for filtering as scale increases.
record.problems: The attack evidence is measured through medical text loss rather than targeted-knowledge accuracy. The paper does not report uncertainty for the attack results; figure values are not numerically tabulated. The tested relearning data are in-domain medical text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the adversarial-fine-tuning outcomes in Figures 7 and 26.

untested.parts: RMU's forget accuracy near chance and its retained general ability are not reported; only pre-attack forget test loss appears in Figure 26.

Relearning on unrelated or loosely related data. Accuracy-based recovery, since only loss is measured. The attack data (PubMed, Common Pile) is the same domain as RMU's PubMed forget set; overlap is not stated.
Not tested. In-context retrieval weakness of filtering is only cited from O'Brien et al.
Filtering's robustness to prompting, in-context, quantization or internal-edit attacks.

missing.what: The headline claim that filtering is 'up to 10×' more robust than RMU at 1.8B, which differs from the 13× reported for token removal in §4.3
The attack learning rate was chosen per model to reach parity fastest (a strongest-attack selection); this affects the token counts
RMU's retain or general-ability performance after unlearning is not reported; whether RMU preserved retain loss is unknown

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Models are small and trained from scratch on a medical proxy, not WMDP. Recovery is measured as medical text loss reaching unfiltered-baseline parity, not as accuracy. For filtered models, 'recovery' means learning knowledge never acquired, so their token counts measure acquisition cost rather than recovery of hidden knowledge. The single-state field forces RMU rows to carry B's state; for A, the same rows show resistance absent.

versions.untested_parts: Tests whether fine-tuning recovers performance after RMU, but does not report RMU accuracy near chance or retained general ability in the attacked setup.
Tests adversarial fine-tuning on medical text; it does not test unrelated or loosely related examples, a subset of forgotten facts, or a stated small relearning-set size.
Activation-direction ablation and evidence that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting are not tested.
Prompt rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context recovery are not tested.
Tests pretraining data filtering against adversarial fine-tuning on medical text; it does not test resistance to activation edits, quantization, or prompting attacks.

source_check.notes: Loss-only measure on PubMed text. Most rows are figure-only (Figs 7, 26); only the 1.8B ratios (1.5x, 3x, 13x) are in the text, and Fig 7's falling share of pretraining holds for every method, RMU most steeply. The 10.73 in Fig 26 is most plausibly RMU's start loss, but no panel is named. Filtered models were trained on FineWeb-Edu; PubMed is only attack and test data.

statements.correction: The study's references are document-filtered, token-loss-masked and token-removed models (61M-1816M, from scratch), all given the same PubMed fine-tuning attack as RMU.

Adversarial fine-tuning on PubMed text runs only until baseline loss parity, with the learning rate chosen for the fewest steps (effective batch size 40,960). Per Fig 26, RMU's loss 'steeply improves in just a couple steps'. Absolute token counts are figure-only.
statements.problem: The study is grouped under 'large relearning sets', which the text does not support. Its RMU recovery is fast: loss falls steeply within a couple of steps.

statements.correction: One attack only: AdamW fine-tuning on PubMed text, with LR and weight decay swept and the fastest-to-parity setting kept. r21 is RMU's token cost relative to filtering at 1.8B. Drop the citation.
statements.problem: The study is cited (r21) for attack-method sensitivity, but it reports no comparison across optimizers, objectives or fine-tuned parameters.

statements.correction: Fig 7: for every method, larger models need fewer fine-tuning tokens as a share of pretraining; RMU's curve is the steepest.

Token-level filtering (loss masking, removal) on 61M-1816M from-scratch models, PubMed fine-tuning attack, loss measure: at 1.8B it needs 3x and 13x RMU's tokens to reach baseline loss, and loss falls more gradually than RMU's. All models still reach baseline loss.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: RMU under adversarial fine-tuning on PubMed medical text
reader_labels.reason: RMU fine-tuning restores baseline medical loss; the paper says loss falls steeply after a couple of steps (r1, r5, r9, r13, r17, r21, r25, r29, r33, r37, r41, r45). The study does not test the near-chance-accuracy or retained-general-ability parts of A.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Fine-tuning reaches baseline performance, and RMU improves steeply after only a few steps; this is evidence of in-domain recovery, not of recovery from unrelated or loosely related examples (r1, r5, r9, r13, r17, r21, r25, r29, r33, r37, r41, r45).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Document and token filtering under medical adversarial fine-tuning
reader_labels.reason: Filtered models require more adversarial fine-tuning than RMU to reach baseline, including 1.5×, 3× and 13× more tokens at 1816M; their loss trajectories are more gradual (r2-r4, r6-r8, r10-r12, r14-r16, r18-r20, r22-r24, r26-r28, r30-r32, r34-r36, r38-r40, r42-r44, r46-r48).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The evidence is limited to adversarial fine-tuning using medical text; filtering does not prevent eventual recovery to baseline in that setup, and other attack types are untested (r2-r4, r22-r24, r26-r28, r46-r48).
